entries.title: Zizou Bergs stuns Alcaraz in Shanghai as Zverev claims year-end top ranking
entries.summary: After defending his Japan Open title after returning from injury, Alcaraz never found his rhythm in a scrappy contest.
entries.content:
Fresh from defending his Japan Open title after returning from injury, Alcaraz never found his rhythm in a scrappy contest.

Seven-time Grand Slam champion Carlos Alcaraz has suffered a shock 7-5 7-6(4) defeat by unseeded Belgian Zizou Bergs in the Shanghai Masters round of 32, a result ⁠that also confirmed Alexander Zverev as the ATP’s year-end world number one.

Fresh from defending his Japan Open title and building momentum after a lengthy wrist injury layoff, Alcaraz never found his rhythm in a scrappy two-hour, two-minute contest on Monday.

The second-seeded Spaniard, who ⁠was sidelined for nearly five months before returning at the US Open in late August and reaching the quarterfinals, joined 24-time Grand Slam champion Novak Djokovic and US Open runner-up Ben Shelton among the high-profile casualties at the ATP Masters 1000 event.

Bergs produced a composed all-court performance, thriving in the quick conditions as the 27-year-old broke Alcaraz’s serve three times to clinch the ‌biggest victory of his career.

Bergs had lost their only previous meeting, falling to Alcaraz in the last 16 of last year’s Japan Open, but showed no signs of intimidation as he outplayed the 23-year-old in key moments.

“This is something that has been very tough for me,” Bergs said, when asked about getting a win against one of the biggest names on the ATP Tour.

“I often have too much respect for these guys, which is part of my culture and I’m proud of that. But it gets a little bit in the way when you have to ⁠play them…

“The more experience you have practising against them and playing matches, the more it ⁠becomes the new standard a little bit. To have this moment, for me it is a little bit of a relief. I feel like now I really can win against these guys.”

‘Dream come true’

The upset also guaranteed French Open and US Open champion Zverev, 29, the ATP’s year-end world ⁠number one ranking, making him the first German and the oldest first-time player to achieve the feat.

Zverev’s route to the top spot opened after Italian Jannik Sinner had not played ⁠since beating him in the Wimbledon final on July 12 due to a ⁠knee injury.

The 25-year-old Sinner missed the North American hard-court tournaments, the US Open and the ongoing Asian contests. The five-times major winner will also sit out the European indoor season and the ATP Finals in Turin, where he has lifted the trophy in each of the last two years.

“It’s been a ‌fantastic season for me winning in Paris and New York and knowing that I will finish the year on top of the rankings is just a dream come true,” said Zverev, who will face Kazakhstan’s 19th seed Alexander Bublik in the ‌round ‌of 16 in Shanghai.

“So much work and effort have been put into achieving this goal, especially after coming back from the ankle injury [at the 2022 French Open semifinals].

“I look forward to finishing the season in style.”

entries.title: Israeli academic and Al Jazeera contributor Ori Goldberg dies at 50
entries.summary: Goldberg was a regular Al Jazeera contributor and died after a long battle with colon cancer, his family said.
entries.content:
Goldberg, a regular Al Jazeera contributor, died after a long battle with colon cancer, his family says in a statement.

Israeli academic and independent analyst Ori Goldberg has died at the age of 50, his family has said.

His eldest daughter Avigail confirmed his death after a long battle with colon cancer in a statement on Goldberg’s X account on Sunday.

“In one sentence, he was the best dad in the world. But you can’t really describe him in one sentence, and I don’t think I’ll have the courage to try,” she wrote.

In a separate post on Goldberg’s X account, his eldest son, identified as Dave, said his father was “the light where things looked dark”.

Goldberg was a frequent contributor to Al Jazeera’s website where his opinion pieces focused on Middle East affairs.

In his final piece for the Qatar-based media network last month, he wrote about Israeli authorities’ reaction to the award-winning documentary NAZA, by Yuval Avraham and Rachel Szor.

In a memorable piece titled Israel is imploding in December 2025, he explored whether Israel could be losing its status as regional hegemon while the Israeli state and society become increasingly dysfunctional.

“An international coalition, led by the United States with the participation of Qatar, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, is gradually removing Gaza from Israel’s control, as well as pressuring Israel out of its territorial escapades in Syria and Lebanon,” he wrote.

In another piece from the same month titled Netanyahu will win again he explained why the Israeli prime minister’s supporters would likely vote for him in a 2026 election.

“He is ‘their’ man, the one who represents them against the elites who feel the country is theirs by right. He alone, through his audacity and cunning, took the fight to Israel’s enemies and brought them to their knees.” he wrote. “[Netanyahu] is the one who broke the paradigm that put Israel at the mercy of the world. Israel now does as it wishes, and those desires are for Israel alone to articulate”.

Goldberg also appeared regularly on Al Jazeera English news and current affairs shows including Inside Story.

He received a PhD in History from Tel Aviv University in 2008 and wrote his dissertation on the role of religious experience in the creation and application of Iranian Shia revolutionary discourse during the second half of the 20th century.

He received many awards and scholarships, including a fellowship at the Mellon Foundation from 2013 to 2015.

entries.title: What are the key matches to watch as the UEFA Champions League returns?
entries.summary: Atletico vs Man United and Man City vs PSG headline the league's match day two action as the competition returns.
entries.content:
Atletico vs Man United and Man City vs PSG headline the Champions League match day two action as the competition returns.

The UEFA Champions League (UCL) 2026-27 enters its second round of matches this week, with 36 teams in action across Europe as clubs return to the elite football competition.

After the first set of league fixtures, two-time title holders Paris Saint-Germain lead the points table with three points, followed by six-time champions Bayern Munich and five-time winners Barcelona, who also won their opening matches.

The competition’s league phase format, now in its third year, started in September and runs until January 2027. It will be followed by the knockout rounds, with the champions crowned in early June.

Here’s all you need to know about this year’s competition:

What is the Champions League?

The Champions League is an annual club competition that features the best teams from across Europe.

This season marks the third time that 36 teams will participate in the main round, an increase from 32 under the old format.

What is the 2026-27 Champions League format?

Since 2003, the UCL has featured 32 clubs split into eight groups of four, with the top two from each section advancing to the last 16.

That has changed radically in recent years.

From the 2024-25 season, the 36 clubs are pooled into a single league in a “Swiss system” more commonly associated with chess.

Earlier, participating teams played six games in the group stage, facing each opponent home and away. Now, each club plays eight games, one each against eight different opponents.

How does the Champions League knockout format work?

At the end of the league phase, the top eight qualify directly for the knockouts, while those between the ninth and 24th places have to compete in two-legged knockout-phase playoffs.

Teams ranked 25th and below are eliminated.

The UCL knockout format is straightforward – it begins with the round of 16, followed by the quarterfinals, semifinals and the final.

When are the league phase and knockout matches?

The league phase matches are scheduled for:

  • Match day 1: September 8-10
  • Match day 2: October 13 and 14
  • Match day 3: October 20 and 21
  • Match day 4: November 3 and 4
  • Match day 5: November 24 and 25
  • Match day 6: December 8 and 9
  • Match day 7: January 19 and 20
  • Match day 8: January 27

The knockout phase matches are scheduled for (all dates in 2027):

  • Playoffs: February 16, 17 and 23, 24
  • Round of 16: March 9, 10 and 16, 17
  • Quarterfinals: April 6, 7 and 13, 14
  • Semifinals: April 27, 28 and May 4, 5
  • Final: June 5

Which are the best Champions League matches to watch?

The key matches to follow on matchdays two and three are as follows:

Top five UCL matches to watch this week

  • Arsenal vs Lille, Tuesday 19:00 GMT
  • Atletico vs Manchester United, Tuesday 19:00 GMT
  • Galatasaray vs Barcelona, Tuesday 19:00 GMT
  • Manchester City vs PSG, Wednesday 19:00 GMT
  • AS Roma vs Real Madrid, Wednesday 19:00 GMT

Top five Champions League matches to watch next week:

  • PSG vs Barcelona, October 20, 19:00 GMT
  • Liverpool vs Villarreal, October 20, 19:00 GMT
  • Como vs Manchester United, October 21, 16:45 GMT
  • Bayern Munich vs Arsenal, October 21, 19:00 GMT
  • Real Madrid vs RB Leipzig, October 21, 19:00 GMT

What are the key UCL storylines to follow?

Man City’s home clash with PSG headlines the upcoming round of matches, marking the troubled Etihad club’s first Champions League match since an independent commission found them guilty of breaking more than 100 Premier League financial rules.

Elsewhere, City’s crosstown rivals, under-fire Man United, are also in action this week. They head to Madrid to face an in-form Atletico, hoping to register just their third win this season.

Meanwhile, manager Jose Mourinho will face his former club AS Roma when Real travel to the Italian capital.

Who are the top players to watch in the Champions League?

PSG’s Ferran Torres, who scored a hat-trick in the first UCL match, is a joint top scorer in this year’s UCL alongside Ermedin Demirovic of Stuttgart.

Also watch out for Man City’s Erling Haaland, Bayern Munich’s talented Michael Olise and PSG forward Ousmane Dembele, all of whom scored two goals in their respective UCL openers.

entries.title: At least 20 injured in northern Israel explosion
entries.summary: The blast has been caused by unexploded ordnance in northern Israel near the Lebanese border.
entries.content:
The blast was caused by unexploded ordnance in northern Israel near the Lebanese border.

A blast caused by unexploded ordnance in northern Israel near the Lebanese border has injured approximately 20 people, police say.

Israel’s Magen David Adom said paramedics were treating “eight casualties in serious and moderate condition, as well as several additional casualties in mild condition” following the explosion on Monday, which police said occurred near the community of Neot Mordechai, between Kibbutz Manara and Kibbutz Yiftach.

Police officers from the Kiryat Shmona station (Northern District) are on-site, securing and cordoning off the area, while bomb disposal experts investigate the circumstances and source of the explosion.

Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank said, the explosion happened around several Israelis who were on a picnic or a hike in the area, on the border with Lebanon, adding that some of the injured are described to be in critical condition.

“There is very little specific information as to what happened, what the source of that explosion was, but it’s certainly a reminder that Northern Israel, the upper Galilee and particularly the border with Lebanon remains an area where there is a military operation, with the Israeli military deployed and where thousands of munitions were used over the past 3 years”, Odeh said.

Odeh said the explosion had “mobilised” Israel’s political echelons, with the Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu heading to the area, and the Israeli minister of National Security National Ben Gvir canceling a political engagement that was on his agenda.

entries.title: Confronting the ‘largest energy security threat’
entries.summary: The head of the International Energy Agency, Fatih Birol, discusses the challenges facing the global economy.
entries.content:
Talk to Al Jazeera

Confronting the ‘largest energy security threat’

The head of the International Energy Agency, Fatih Birol, discusses the challenges facing the global economy.

The head of the International Energy Agency (IEA) says we are facing the biggest energy crisis ever.

More than seven months on, it continues with little relief in sight. The US-Israel war on Iran is driving the crisis, which has disrupted global shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for 20 percent of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas.

That has sent fuel prices soaring, interrupted supply chains and raised fears of a serious energy shortage.

IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol says global oil stocks are declining fast. G7 countries and members of the IEA have tapped into their strategic emergency reserves. But relief has been short-lived and the global economy is still feeling the pain.

The Russia-Ukraine war is putting additional strain on the oil industry, as both countries target each other’s energy facilities.

Birol says if tensions in the Middle East are not resolved, it could have serious consequences for the world economy. He warns of challenging months ahead as winter approaches in the Northern Hemisphere.

Birol says it will take time for the energy sector to recover from this crisis, and he acknowledges the industry will likely never be the same again.

entries.title: Nobel economics prize awarded to Robert Hall and Michael ⁠Woodford
entries.summary: The Swedish academy says the academics' models are 'now used by central banks and ​governments around the world'.
entries.content:
The Swedish academy says the academics’ models are ‘now used by central banks and ​governments around the world’.

The ⁠2026 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences has been awarded to US academics Robert Hall and Michael ⁠Woodford for their work on how monetary and fiscal policy can help stabilise fluctuations in the economy, according to the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences.

The winners of the prestigious award, formally known ⁠as the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel and the final prize to be given out this year, were announced on Monday.

The two laureates developed new macroeconomic models that improve people’s ability to implement effective stabilisation policies, enabling fiscal and monetary policy measures that can reduce damaging swings in the economy.

“The laureates’ work has provided us ‌with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world,” John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said in a statement.

“With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume.”

During the oil crises in the 1970s, the existing Keynesian models used to determine when and how measures should be implemented to tackle recessions or other economic fluctuations stopped working. Hall and Woodford then developed new tools to understand what policy responses could be the most effective.

“Rather than basing the models on statistical links between macroeconomic variables, such as inflation, production and consumption, they chose to build them on a microeconomic foundation,” the academy said. “This encompasses an understanding of how the total mass of individual households and businesses affect the economy through their actions.”

The economics prize, first awarded ⁠in 1969, is not part of the five original awards ⁠created in the 1895 will of industrialist and dynamite inventor Alfred Nobel, but was instead established by Sweden’s central bank.

The majority of previous laureates have been from the United States. Only three women have ⁠ever won, most recently Claudia Goldin in 2023 for her work on how gender has affected pay and employment over time ⁠in the US.

Last year’s winners – Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt – won for ‌their work on “creative destruction” and how new technology and production methods can boost growth and living standards.

Like the other Nobel awards, the economics prize consists of a diploma, a gold medal, and a $1.2m cheque.

The Nobel prizes for medicine, physics, chemistry, literature and peace were announced last ‌week, with South African jurist Navi Pillay and Canadian writer Anne Carson among the winners.

entries.title: Trump thinks Ukraine needs a new president. Who could replace Zelenskyy?
entries.summary: Popular former general Zaluzhnyi leads potential challengers, alongside intelligence chief Budanov and reformer Fedorov.
entries.content:
Popular former general Zaluzhnyi leads potential challengers, alongside intelligence chief Budanov and reformer Fedorov.

Kyiv, Ukraine – The White House wants Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy gone.

“I think it’s ⁠⁠time for Ukraine to get a new president,” United States President Donald Trump told reporters on Saturday, claiming that Zelenskyy’s months-long strikes on Russian refineries had hurt global diesel supplies.

But Trump’s wish is not Ukraine’s command.

Even though Zelenskyy’s five-year presidential term expired in 2024, Ukraine’s constitution and martial law grant him a wartime extension. Many Ukrainians want their political establishment to be renewed, but are reluctant to see a presidential vote before the four-and-a-half year war is over.

In response to Trump’s remarks, Zelenskyy proposed holding a vote if Russian President Vladimir Putin guaranteed a 60-day ceasefire.

However, if the elections are held in the near future, who could compete with Zelenskyy?

“If the elections are held fast, one of the former military [commanders] is Zelenskyy’s most probable rival,” Kyiv-based analyst Igar Tyshkevych told Al Jazeera.

Meanwhile, old political heavyweights such as former President Viktor Poroshenko, who lost the 2019 presidential vote to Zelenskyy, and former Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko, who is being investigated for corruption, do not stand a chance, he said.

Valerii Zaluzhnyi: ‘Most probable alternative’

Ukraine’s former top general and current ambassador to the United Kingdom tops the lists of Zelenskyy’s rivals.

“At least since 2023, and especially since 2024, after his resignation, the most probable alternative to Zelenskyy, his most dangerous competitor who can defeat him in the election is Valerii Zaluzhnyi,” Volodymyr Fesenko, head of the Kyiv-based Penta think tank, told Al Jazeera.

Almost two-thirds of Ukrainians – 64 percent – trust him, according to an October 8 poll by the Rating Group, a Kyiv-based pollster, and only 25 percent “distrust” him.

This trust is rooted in his 2022 military triumphs.

After defending Kyiv in the early weeks of Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion, Zaluzhnyi led counteroffensives that returned 40 percent of Russian-controlled territory to Ukraine.

He was fired in 2023 after a long-anticipated summer counteroffensive yielded no results.

Zaluzhnyi remains a man of mystery when it comes to the most pressing postwar matters.

Burly and imposing, the 53-year-old is deliberately taciturn, leaving the public guessing about his views on Ukraine’s economic restoration, crippling demographic crisis or push to join the European Union.

He does not take part in talk shows, barely talks to journalists and occasionally publishes opinion pieces with detailed analyses of war-related problems and general statements about securing lasting peace and security guarantees from Ukraine’s Western partners.

Zelenskyy’s second chance?

The former comedian was elected in 2019 with 73 percent of the vote, the highest result in Ukraine’s post-Soviet history.

Despite a string of corruption scandals in his inner circle, the 48-year-old is popular enough to take another swing at a presidency.

More than half of Ukrainians – 53 percent – trust him, although 40 percent do not, according to the Rating Group’s poll.

However, Trump’s renewed animosity may benefit Zelenskyy again.

After his February 2025 row with Trump in the Oval Office, Zelenskyy’s approval ratings hit a wartime high of 67 percent.

However, Zelenskyy may have ruined his own chances with his appointment policies.

“He came to power under the slogans of resetting the power, of picking the most competent, not the most trusted” ministers or advisers, analyst Tyshkevych said.

Kyrylo Budanov: Trusted by more than half of Ukrainians

Lt. Gen. Kyrylo Budanov is the second most popular and charismatic military leader who has a shot at becoming Ukraine’s president.

The 40-year-old former top military intelligence officer was appointed head of Zelenskyy’s administration in January.

Budanov led daring operations against Russia, including a raid on Russian-annexed Crimea in 2016 to plant explosives at a military airfield.

In 2020, Zelenskyy appointed him head of the defence ministry’s intelligence directorate (GUR), which became an aggressive, tech-driven special forces service.

The GUR’s sea drone attacks damaged Russia’s Black Sea Fleet, forcing it to retreat from annexed Crimea to the Russian port of Novorossiysk.

Budanov is trusted by 53 percent of Ukrainians and mistrusted by 31 percent, according to the Rating Group’s poll.

Mykhailo Fedorov: Young, popular, daring

At 35, Fedorov is the youngest person on the list of potential presidents. He rose to fame after Zelenskyy appointed him minister of digital transformation in 2019, and managed to radically simplify bureaucratic procedures in the corruption-plagued nation. His ministry launched Diia, a smartphone app that lets users access more than 100 government services online.

In January, Zelenskyy appointed Fedorov, who had zero military background, as defence minister in charge of logistics, budgets, reforms, anticorruption measures and deals to secure multibillion-dollar Western aid or loans.

Fedorov cracked down on corruption schemes by making procurement of new weaponry, food and medical supplies more transparent.

He radically boosted the number of drones that paralysed Russia’s supply routes, destroyed arms and fuel depots, oil refineries and air defence systems.

He also increased the number of ground robots to supply food and ammunition and rescue wounded soldiers.

But the reforms angered Oleksandr Syrsky, the actual commander-in-chief, who reportedly pushed for Fedorov’s dismissal in July.

Fedorov’s supporters rallied throughout Ukraine for weeks, while his approval ratings soared from 35 percent in June to 65 percent in July, according to the Rating Group’s polls.

However, in August he made an unpopular move saying Ukraine should hold a presidential vote, and his current approval stands at 38 percent.

Yevhenii Khmara: Ukraine’s unknown defence minister

The top five list ends with Yevhenii Khmara, a general who replaced Fedorov as defence minister.

A relative unknown until his appointment in July, he is trusted by 29 percent of Ukrainians and distrusted by 16 percent.

He was a career intelligence official with a low public profile, but another 43 percent of those polled did not know who he was, according to the survey.

Low hopes for a foreign minister and an ex-president

Numbers six and seven on the list are Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, a career diplomat who secured crucial support from Turkiye and Poland, and ex-president Poroshenko.

Both are trusted by 24 percent of Ukrainians.

But Poroshenko, who came to power in 2014 on an anti-corruption ticket but got involved in a graft scandal with overpriced spare parts for military equipment, holds a low popularity rating – 70 percent of those polled distrust him.

entries.title: Which banners did Liverpool fans display at Anfield against Man City?
entries.summary: From creative wordplay on song lyrics to simply calling Man City 'cheats', the Reds fans went all out at Anfield.
entries.content:
From creative wordplay on song lyrics to simply calling Man City ‘cheats’, the Reds fans went all out at Anfield.

It was billed as one of the most emotionally charged club football matches in recent years with Liverpool’s historically vocal and disapproving fans promising a hostile reception for Manchester City as the Blues played their first match after being found guilty of breaching the Premier League’s financial rules.

In the end, Manchester City walked away from it with three points in the bag and smiles on their faces but not without facing scorn from the Reds’ supporters at their famed Anfield Stadium in Liverpool.

The Blues evaded a much-anticipated “Anfield welcome” by avoiding the route usually taken by team buses driving into the venue. Instead, City’s bus was driven into the stadium via a different route and entrance, usually reserved for service vehicles on match days.

While Enzo Maresca’s team avoided the flares, pyrotechnics and attacks on the bus that were meted out to City during their visit to Anfield for a UEFA Champions League match eight years ago, there was no escaping the chants and banners inside the stadium.

The creativity of Liverpool fans was displayed on the streets lined with thousands of Reds fans before kickoff and inside Anfield once they unfurled their scathing banners in the stands.

Here’s a selection of the best banners and signs displayed inside Anfield on Sunday:

The most direct attacks since the Premier League’s independent commission’s guilty verdict was announced have focused on the finding that City “arranged ‘sham’ contracts” with a number of its commercial partners.

Man City were found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges, giving Liverpool fans the chance to create a wide, strip-like banner that carried the word “cheats” but with the British pound sign replacing the “e” 115 times. The banner was held across the stand behind City’s goal.

Liam Gallagher, lead vocalist of the British rock band Oasis, is a self-admitted lifelong Man City fan. Gallagher has been vocal in his support for City despite the charges and was among the travelling Blues supporters at Anfield. Liverpool fans picked on lyrics from some of Oasis’s biggest hits and creatively used them to mock City. The banner above takes a line from the hit song Stop Crying Your Heart Out.

A little creativity was needed for this banner, which carried a stanza from the song Where Did It All Go Wrong? A number of the titles that City won during the charged 2009-2018 period were with teams built around global football stars.

Liverpool’s supporters were among many in the Premier League who felt “cheated” during the years that City piled up domestic football trophies. They made no secret of their feelings when given the chance at Anfield against Man City.

Liverpool fans mocked the empire built by City’s former manager Pep Guardiola, who signed some of the biggest names during his decade-long run at the helm, which brought 20 trophies.

Manchester City fans had their own way of mocking Liverpool. They waved inflatable bananas at the away end, a reference to a decades-long tradition when a City fan took a blow-up banana to a game in 1987. It also served as a dig at then-Liverpool captain Steven Gerrard, who slipped during a match against Chelsea in the 2013-2014 season when the 0-2 loss to the London club set off a series of results that saw City clinch a come-from-behind Premier League title.
